The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "The Most Timeless NBA Plays": https://pudding.cool/2017/05/nba-moments/
The files: data/plays.csv, data/curated_merged_by_decade.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data files and reading the story.

The Most Timeless NBA plays
The Most Timeless
# NBA plays
# Historic NBA games and plays, ranked by YouTube views
By Russell Samora
and Matt Daniels
T-mac's 13 points in 35 seconds is the greatest-ever human feat to transpire on a basketball
court.
And by greatest-ever, we mean people still watch clips of this moment, thirteen years later, marveling
at its glory.
This idea facinates us: from the vault of all NBA clips, what has stood the test of time? Do Jordan
highlights dominate the ‘85 - ‘96 era, overshadowing whatever feats accomplished by Bird or Magic? Do people
still watch Reggie Miller’s 8 points in 9 seconds? Or Big Shot Rob’s many game-winners?
Using view counts from YouTube (provided by Google News Lab), we
aggregated hundreds of thousands of videos by game and player in order to rank historic NBA moments by
present-day popularity. First, let's look at what's viewed from the oughts.
Most-viewed: 2000 - 2009
#1 T-mac's 13 points in 33 seconds (Dec 9, 2004 - 27M views)
#2 Kobe scores 81 (Jan 22, 2006 - 22M views)
#3 Jordan ball fakes (Apr 7, 2003 – 9.4M views)
#4 Fisher's 0.4 second game-winner (May 13, 2004 – 7.8M views)
#5 Iverson steps over Lue (Jun 6, 2001 – 6M views)
There, it's settled: T-mac at #1. The rest of the data checks out too: Fisher's game-winner at #4.
Here's the rest of the top 100 in a fully explorable chart with accompaying videos.
Most of these plays are already legendary, hard-coded into our brain’s NBA memory vault. But some are new to
us, finding a second life on YouTube.
It’s worth watching #8 Wade’s Dunk on Varejao and #10
Nate Robinson blocks Yao . Let's move onto the ‘90s, arguably the most divisive era for
debating timelessness.
Most-viewed: 1990 - 1999
#1 Jordan's last 3 minutes as a Bull (Jun 14, 1998 - 35M views)
#2 Jordan blocks Shaq in first meeting (Jan 12, 1993 - 12M views)
#3 Shaq brings down the backboard (Apr 23, 1993 – 11M views)
#4 Jordan's eyes-closed free-throw (Nov 23, 1991 – 6.5M views)
#5 Jordan's "Flu Game" (Jun 11, 1997 – 6.5M views)
It's not that suprising to see Jordan's historic moment at #1. It has more views than any other
NBA moment in our dataset (i.e., it's #1, all-time, at 35M views). But the rest of the top 5 have much to be
desired. The #2 play, a Jordan block on Shaq, is more symbolic than impresive. And we're very disappointed
to see Reggie's 8 points in 9 seconds outside the top 5 (it's #6).
More than half of the plays are Jordan highlights. Yes, the G.O.A.T. should understandly be popular on YouTube,
yet we were hoping for more Barkley, Malone, or Olajuwon. It's criminal that there's only one Ewing
highlight, and it's him on the receiving end of a Jordan dunk (maybe rings, for historical relevance,
truly do matter?)
Finally, let's examine the ‘80s, an era with so many great moments that they were enshrined with
names (i.e., "The Shot")
Most-viewed: 1980 - 1989
#1 The Shot (May 7, 1989 - 5.8M views)
#2 Jordan scores 63 (Apr 20, 1986 - 3.2M views)
#3 Bird steals pass for game-winner (May 26, 1987 – 2M views)
#4 Bird scores 60 vs. Hawks (Mar 12, 1985 – 1.8M views)
#5 Jordan's first 40-point game (Nov 13, 1984 – 1.2M views)
Unsurprisingly, 3 of the top 5 are Jordan. Bird at #3 is satisfying, especially given the historic significance
of the steal (1987 conf. playoffs, game 5).
In our research for this project, we dug up experts' lists of top 10 plays from the ‘80s. They
pointed to moments such as Ralph Sampson's game-winner (#26) , Tree Bites Man (#31) , or The Sleepy Floyd Game (#42) ,
not Jordan's first 40-point game (#5) .
That's not to discount Jordan’s accomplishments, but we worry that other, non-Jordan feats are being
overshadowed by our present-day obsession with the G.O.A.T. (or perhaps we can blame Nike's marketing
engine, which keeps him in the cultural zeitgeist).
We barely found any videos in our top 100 from pre-Jordan era (‘80 - ‘84). And we wonder how fans
will remember the impact of Dr. J, Kareem, or Larry Bird when basketball history begins in 1985.
We appreciate Google Newslab for collaborating on this project
and providing data to complete the analysis. The full version, all data 1980 - 2017, is here. Each graphic is also fully embeddable; just click
the "embed this" link.
